entities.name: Lucius Aemilius Paullus Macedonicus
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Lucius Aemilius Paullus Macedonicus (died 159 BCE) stands as a towering figure of the Roman Republic's mid-2nd century BCE, a period marked by its aggressive expansion across the Hellenistic East. A scion of the influential Aemilia gens, his military and political career culminated in the decisive conquest of the Antigonid kingdom of Macedon during the Third Macedonian War (171–168 BCE), permanently dismantling the last major successor state of Alexander the Great's empire and solidifying Rome's dominance over the Greek world. His actions irrevocably altered the geopolitical landscape of the Mediterranean, ushering in an era of direct Roman provincial rule in the Balkans and Greece.

Despite initial electoral setbacks and a reputation for strict discipline, Paullus was elected consul for the second time in 168 BCE, specifically to resolve the protracted Third Macedonian War. He decisively defeated King Perseus of Macedon at the Battle of Pydna on June 22, 168 BCE, a victory that saw an estimated 20,000 Macedonian soldiers killed and Perseus captured. Following the battle, Paullus meticulously reorganized Macedon into four separate, tribute-paying republics, ensuring its fragmentation and preventing any resurgence of royal power. He subsequently plundered Epirus, leading to the enslavement of 150,000 people and the destruction of 70 towns, a punitive measure designed to deter future resistance to Roman authority.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Lucius Aemilius Paullus Macedonicus's victory at Pydna fundamentally ended the Antigonid kingdom and secured Rome's dominance over the Greek world, leading to a century of direct tax exemption for Roman citizens due to the immense plunder. His actions solidified Rome's regional hegemony and deeply influenced its future expansion and economic structure.
